unitTitle: ISAs, Operating Systems, and Virtual Memory
overview: This unit compares x86, RISC-V, and ARM in terms of their registers, calling conventions (Aufrufkonventionen), addressing modes (Adressierungsarten), and instruction formats (Befehlsformen). It explains how multiuser systems (Mehrbenutzersysteme) use privileged modes (privilegierte Modi), a scheduler (Scheduler), and interrupts (Unterbrechungen) to control program execution. Virtual memory (virtueller Speicher), the MMU, page tables (Seitentabellen), and the TLB translate addresses and enforce access permissions; lazy allocation (Lazy Allocation) and paging (Paging) provide pages on demand or evict them.

entries.short: x86 is a CISC ISA family with complex instructions, variable instruction lengths, and multiple execution modes.
entries.explanation: x86 denotes a family of closely related but distinct ISAs. In the example shown, instructions are 1 to 7 bytes long; this variable length differs from the mostly 4-byte RISC-V instructions considered here. The family supports legacy execution modes and reflects a long history of accumulated complexity.
entries.example: In the examples shown, an x86 instruction can be 1 byte or several bytes long.
pitfalls: x86 does not denote a single word size.
Variable instruction length says nothing about register width.
entries.heading: IA-32 und die x86-Familie

entries.short: IA-32 denotes the 32-bit ISA of the x86 family.
entries.explanation: IA-32 is the 32-bit variant of the x86 family, introduced with the Intel 80386 and continued in processors including the 80486 and Pentium. It has eight general-purpose registers. In the calling convention described here, parameters are placed on the stack and the return value is in EAX.
entries.example: `cc -m32` selects 32-bit output for the program shown.
pitfalls: IA-32 is not the 64-bit extension x86_64.
A 32-bit ISA does not mean that every instruction is 32 bits long.
related: Registers and subregister views in x86
entries.heading: IA-32 und die x86-Familie

entries.short: x86_64, also known as Intel 64, is the 64-bit extension of the x86 family, originally developed by AMD.
entries.explanation: x86_64 extends the x86 family to 64 bits and adds registers R8 through R15, among other features. AMD originally developed the extension; Intel calls its compatible implementation Intel 64. New word sizes were added through new execution modes, while older modes remained supported.
entries.example: RAX is the 64-bit view of the register whose 32-bit view is called EAX.
pitfalls: Intel 64 is not the original source of the 64-bit x86 extension.
x86_64 and IA-32 denote different word sizes within the x86 family.
related: Registers and subregister views in x86
entries.heading: IA-32 und die x86-Familie

entries.short: ISA extensions add instructions or capabilities to a processor family.
entries.explanation: VMX supports virtual machines, F16C converts half-precision floating-point values, and Transactional Memory supports speculative execution related to atomic accesses. An extension adds specific features to the existing ISA. Whether it is available depends on the processor.
entries.example: VMX provides features for supporting virtual machines.
pitfalls: An extension is not necessarily present in every x86 processor.
Here, F16C refers to conversion instructions.
entries.heading: Genannte Erweiterungen von IA-32 / x86

entries.term: Registers and subregister views in x86
entries.short: Several x86 register names refer to views of different widths over the same register storage.
entries.explanation: RAX denotes the 64-bit view, EAX the 32-bit view, AX the 16-bit view, and AH and AL each denote an 8-bit subregister view. IA-32 has eight general-purpose registers; x86_64 adds R8 through R15, for a total of 16. ESP/RSP is the stack pointer, and EBP/RBP serves as the base pointer in the stack frame shown.
entries.example: EAX is the 32-bit view of the register storage denoted by RAX.
pitfalls: These names do not denote four independent registers.
The stated register roles depend on the ISA and calling convention.
entries.heading: Register und Teilsichten

entries.short: A calling convention specifies where parameters and return values are placed and which registers a subroutine must preserve.
entries.explanation: In the IA-32 convention shown, parameters are placed on the stack, the return value is in EAX, and the caller removes the parameters after the return. In the x86_64 convention noted here, the first six parameters are in RDI, RSI, RDX, RCX, R8, and R9, with additional parameters on the stack; the return value is in RAX. RBX, RBP, RSP, and R12 through R15 are listed as callee-saved. The notes do not specify an ABI or operating system, so these details apply to the examples described and not generally to every x86_64 environment.
entries.example: In an x86_64 call with seven integer parameters, six are in the registers listed and the seventh is on the stack.
pitfalls: The register order is not the same in every x86_64 environment.
Callee-saved means that the called subroutine restores a changed register value when necessary.
related: Registers and subregister views in x86
Return address in x86 and RISC-V
entries.heading: Aufrufkonventionen

entries.term: Return address in x86 and RISC-V
entries.short: IA-32 places the return address on the stack during a call, whereas RISC-V typically stores it in ra.
entries.explanation: In IA-32, `call` places the address of the next instruction on the stack. In RISC-V, `jal` stores the return address in the specified destination register, usually `ra`. The return address identifies the instruction position at which execution resumes after the subroutine.
entries.example: A typical RISC-V call using `jal ra, ziel` writes the address after the call to `ra`.
pitfalls: `call` and `jal` use different locations for the return address.
The return address is not a function's return value.
entries.heading: Aufrufkonventionen

entries.short: A C program can be compiled as an IA-32 binary and displayed as assembly code using `objdump`.
entries.explanation: The compiler produces 32-bit output with `-m32`; `-O0` selects the unoptimized version shown. The program can then be run and displayed in Intel syntax in a disassembly using `objdump -M intel -d`. The recorded output of the `count.c` example shown is 45.
entries.example:
```bash
cc -m32 count.c -O0 -o count
./count
objdump -M intel -d count
```
pitfalls: Disassembly shows the compiled program's machine instructions, not its original C source code.
`-m32` selects the target word size, and `-O0` selects the optimization level.
entries.heading: Beispielprogramm übersetzen und ansehen

entries.term: Differences between x86 and RISC-V assembly code
entries.short: The x86 instructions shown can use the destination as both a source and a memory operand, whereas RISC-V typically performs arithmetic operations on registers.
entries.explanation: In an x86 two-operand instruction such as `add edx, eax`, the destination is also a source: the old value of EDX is added to EAX, and the result overwrites EDX. x86 can also perform arithmetic directly on a memory operand. RISC-V typically uses `lw`, `add`, and `sw` for this, since arithmetic instructions use register operands. x86 can set flags with `cmp` and then branch with `jne`; RISC-V can combine the comparison and branch, for example, in `bne`.
entries.example:
```asm
# x86
add DWORD PTR [ebp-0x10], eax

# RISC-V: sinngemäß
lw t0, 0(sp)
add t0, t0, a0
sw t0, 0(sp)
```
pitfalls: An x86 memory operand does not mean that an instruction can have any number of operands in memory.
The flags set by `cmp` are part of the x86 sequence.
entries.heading: Unterschiede im Assemblercode

entries.short: The optimization level affects whether the compiler shown keeps variables in memory or in registers.
entries.explanation: In the `-O0` excerpt, the loop variable and sum are accessed in memory relative to EBP. In the `-O2` excerpt shown, they remain in registers; `xor eax, eax` sets a register to zero, and `test edi, edi` checks a value without changing it. The sum is in EDX, the register for the third parameter of `printf` in the x86_64 convention shown. The excerpts use different loop bounds, so this difference cannot be attributed to the optimization level alone.
entries.example: `xor eax, eax` sets EAX to 0 by applying bitwise exclusive OR to the register and itself.
pitfalls: Register allocation in an optimized example is not a fixed rule for all programs.
The different loop bounds are not necessarily a result of `-O0` versus `-O2`.
related: Registers and subregister views in x86
Differences between x86 and RISC-V assembly code
entries.heading: Die gezeigten Beispiele mit -O0 und -O2

entries.short: An addressing mode specifies how an instruction identifies its operands and, where applicable, computes a memory address.
entries.explanation: With immediate addressing, a constant is part of the instruction; with register addressing, the operand is in a named register. With direct addressing, the memory address is part of the instruction; with register-indirect addressing, it is in a register. Displacement or base-relative addressing adds an offset to a register; scaled indexing adds an index multiplied by the operand size to a base. RISC-V supports immediate and register operands as well as memory accesses using a register plus an offset; scaled indexing is not available by default.
entries.example: `lw a0, 8(a1)` loads from address `a1 + 8` in RISC-V.
pitfalls: With register-indirect addressing, the register contains the address, not necessarily the value being loaded.
The 12 bits in the immediate and displacement fields shown do not apply to all constants in an ISA.
entries.heading: Adressierungsarten – Folien 15–23

entries.short: The effective address is the memory address computed from the operands at run time.
entries.explanation: With base-relative addressing, `EA = Registerinhalt + Offset`. With scaled indexing, `EA = Basis + Index · Operandenlänge`. This calculation can, for example, access an array element using its index.
entries.example: With a base address of 1000, an index of 3, and an operand size of 4 bytes, the result is `EA = 1000 + 3 · 4 = 1012`.
pitfalls: The offset is added; it is not itself the effective address.
With scaled indexing, the distance between elements depends on their operand size.
entries.heading: Adressierungsarten – Folien 15–23

entries.short: An address format describes how many operands an instruction names explicitly and where any other operands are located.
entries.explanation: In a 0-address format, operands are implicit on a stack; in a 1-address format, an accumulator is used implicitly. In a 2-address format, one operand serves as both destination and source, as in `add eax, z`. A 3-address register-register format names two sources and a separate destination; a 3-address memory-memory format processes operands directly in memory. The register-register format fits RISC-V's load/store architecture.
entries.example: In a 3-address register-register format, `add x, y, z` means `x = y + z`.
pitfalls: The number in the name counts explicit address fields, not necessarily all implicit operands.
In a 2-address format, the destination overwrites one of its input values.
entries.heading: Adressformen – Folien 24–30

entries.short: With overlapped addressing, an instruction's destination is also one of its sources.
entries.explanation: This applies to the 2-address format: the instruction first reads the old destination value, processes it with another operand, and writes the result to the same destination. In `add eax, z`, `eax = eax + z` is performed. The destination and one source share the same address field.
entries.example: `add edx, eax` reads EDX and EAX and overwrites EDX with their sum.
pitfalls: The result overwrites the old value in the destination register.
The term describes the destination-source relationship, not every memory access in general.
related: Differences between x86 and RISC-V assembly code
entries.heading: Adressformen – Folien 24–30

entries.short: ARMv8 in its AArch64 form is ARM's first 64-bit ISA.
entries.explanation: ARM designs processor architectures and licenses them to partners that manufacture processors. AArch64 shares RISC-V's RISC approach, fixed 4-byte instructions, and load/store architecture. ARM also supports pre-decrement and post-increment, a barrel shifter, conditional execution, and flags. In the register convention described, x0 through x7 are argument registers, x0 is also the return register, x19 through x28 are callee-saved, x29 is the frame pointer, and x30 is the link register; w0 is the 32-bit view of x0.
entries.example: `stp x29, x30, [sp, #-16]!` stores two registers and updates the stack pointer using pre-decrement.
pitfalls: `xzr` and `sp` are special register names, not additional general-purpose registers from x0 through x30.
These register roles apply to the calling convention described.
entries.heading: ARM – Folien 31–38

entries.short: Time sharing divides processor time among programs by having the operating system save and switch their states.
entries.explanation: When the operating system interrupts a running program, it saves its state, especially its registers, stack pointer, and program counter. The scheduler selects the next program; that program's saved state is then loaded and execution resumes. This allows several programs to share a processor in turn.
entries.example: After a timer interrupt, the scheduler can switch from program A to program B.
pitfalls: The interrupted program's state must be preserved so that it can resume later.
The scheduler selects the next program; it does not translate memory addresses.
entries.heading: Mehrbenutzersysteme – Folien 39–47

entries.term: User and system modes (Benutzer- und Systemmodi)
entries.short: Privileged modes specify which instructions and resources a program may use.
entries.explanation: In user mode, privileged actions such as input/output or access to configuration registers are restricted. In system mode, the operating system can perform such actions and control interrupts. RISC-V distinguishes modes M (Machine), S (Supervisor), and U (User); a controlled return to a less privileged mode uses, for example, `mret` or `sret`.
entries.example: A user program requests an operating system function through a system call instead of directly changing a privileged configuration register.
pitfalls: A user program cannot grant itself system privileges with an ordinary jump.
RISC-V has modes M, S, and U; it does not have only two modes.
entries.heading: Mehrbenutzersysteme – Folien 39–47

entries.short: An interrupt is an asynchronous interruption triggered by an external event.
entries.explanation: An interrupt is not directly tied to the instruction currently being executed; typical triggers include a timer, input/output, or a network event. The hardware typically checks the signal at the end of an instruction cycle. The operating system saves the required state, handles the event, and then resumes execution.
entries.example: A timer interrupt can give the scheduler an opportunity to switch to the next process.
pitfalls: An interrupt is asynchronous; an exception is synchronous and associated with an executed instruction.
Maskable interrupts can be disabled temporarily.
entries.heading: Traps, Interrupts und Exceptions – Folien 48–58

entries.short: An exception is a synchronous interruption associated with the execution of a particular instruction.
entries.explanation: An exception can result from an illegal instruction, a breakpoint, or an invalid memory access. The operating system can terminate the process, emulate the operation, pass the event on, or resume execution after handling it. A system call is also triggered deliberately as an exception.
entries.example: An access to an unmapped virtual page can trigger a page-fault exception.
pitfalls: A synchronous event is not the same as an external, asynchronous interrupt.
Whether division by zero triggers an exception depends on the ISA.
entries.heading: Traps, Interrupts und Exceptions – Folien 48–58

entries.short: In RISC-V, a trap is a control transfer to a privileged handler caused by an interrupt or exception.
entries.explanation: A trap is a control transfer to a trap handler triggered by an interrupt or exception. The handler saves or uses the required execution state, handles the cause, and returns in a controlled manner. In other contexts, “trap” is sometimes used more narrowly for deliberately triggered synchronous events, so the ISA's terminology should be observed.
entries.example: A page fault transfers control to the trap handler, which checks the cause and may load a page.
pitfalls: Trap and interrupt are not interchangeable terms; in RISC-V, an interrupt is one possible cause of a trap.
A trap is not necessarily an error, since a system call can trigger one deliberately.
entries.heading: Traps, Interrupts und Exceptions – Folien 48–58

entries.term: System call in RISC-V (Systemaufruf in RISC-V)
entries.short: A system call passes a controlled request from user mode to the operating system.
entries.explanation: In RISC-V, `ecall` triggers the privileged transition; the call number is usually in `a7` and parameters in `a0` through `a6`, while Linux uses `a0` through `a5` for this. The jump target comes from a privileged register, and the operating system can check the parameters and permissions. This distinguishes a system call from an ordinary subroutine call with an arbitrarily chosen target.
entries.example:
1. Place the number in `a7` and parameters in `a0` through `a6`.
2. Execute `ecall`.
3. The handler checks the request, performs the function, and returns in a controlled manner.
pitfalls: `ecall` is not an ordinary call with an arbitrarily chosen target address.
The operating system can reject a request or report an error.
entries.heading: Traps, Interrupts und Exceptions – Folien 48–58

entries.short: The trap mode determines whether events jump to a shared handler address or to computed interrupt addresses.
entries.explanation: In Direct mode (`MODE = 0`), events go to the base address `BASE`; the cause is stored separately in a register. In Vectored mode (`MODE = 1`), asynchronous interrupts jump to `BASE + 4 · cause`. This gives different interrupt causes different entry points.
entries.example: With `BASE = 0x1000` and `cause = 5`, the vectored entry address is `0x1014`.
pitfalls: The vector formula applies to interrupts in Vectored mode.
In Direct mode, no distinct offset encodes the cause.
entries.heading: Traps, Interrupts und Exceptions – Folien 48–58

entries.short: Virtual memory gives each process its own address space, which the MMU translates into physical addresses during memory accesses.
entries.explanation: The Memory Management Unit (MMU) translates virtual addresses into physical addresses during memory accesses. The operating system controls the mapping and can isolate processes and enforce access permissions. A process's virtual pages can map to physical frames at different locations in memory. By contrast, min/max registers provide only a coarse protection region.
entries.example: Two processes can use the same virtual address while the MMU maps it to different physical frames.
pitfalls: A virtual address is not automatically the same as a physical address.
Page translation does not require a physically contiguous block of memory.
related: Page number, offset, and physical frame
entries.heading: Virtueller Speicher – Folien 59–74

entries.term: Page number, offset, and physical frame
entries.short: A virtual address consists of a page number and an offset, which remains unchanged during translation.
entries.explanation: For a page size of 4 KiB, `4 KiB = 2^12 Byte`, so the offset is 12 bits wide. The virtual page number identifies the virtual page; a page table maps it to a physical page number, or frame. The physical address consists of the physical page number and the same offset.
entries.example: For the virtual address `0x00403ABC`, the offset is `0xABC`; only the page number is translated.
pitfalls: The offset is not changed during a normal page translation.
A virtual page and a physical frame are different regions, even though they have the same size.
entries.heading: Virtueller Speicher – Folien 59–74

entries.short: A page table maps virtual pages to physical frames and stores validity and access permissions.
entries.explanation: An Sv32 page-table entry contains a physical page number as well as status and permission bits. `V` marks the entry as valid; `R`, `W`, and `X` permit reading, writing, and execution. `U` permits access in user mode, `G` marks a global mapping, `A` marks an access as having occurred, and `D` marks a write as having occurred. An invalid entry or an unauthorized access causes an exception.
entries.example: A valid entry with `R=1`, `W=0`, and `X=0` permits reading but not writing or execution.
pitfalls: A valid entry is not automatically permitted for every access type or privilege mode.
`A` and `D` describe access status; they are not read or write permissions.
entries.heading: Virtueller Speicher – Folien 59–74

entries.short: The bits X, W, and R encode, in that order, whether a page is executable, writable, and readable.
entries.explanation: The bit order is `X/W/R`: `001` means read only, `011` means read and write, `100` means execute only, `101` means read and execute, and `111` means read, write, and execute. The patterns `010` and `110` are reserved. `000` does not mark a leaf entry; it is a pointer to the next page-table level.
entries.example: The pattern `101` means `X=1`, `W=0`, `R=1`: reading and execution are allowed, but writing is not.
pitfalls: The bit order is X, W, R, not R, W, X.
`000` is a page-table pointer here; `010` and `110` are reserved.
entries.heading: X/W/R-Kodierung

entries.short: The MMU decomposes a virtual address, checks the page-table entry, and uses it to form a physical address.
entries.explanation: Translation uses the page number and offset and checks validity and access permissions. If the entry is invalid, access in user mode is not permitted, or a write targets a read-only page, an exception is raised. If the checks succeed, the unchanged offset is appended to the physical page number.
entries.example:
1. Split the virtual address into a page number and an offset.
2. Read the page-table base address from a privileged register and locate the appropriate entry.
3. Check validity, privilege, and read/write/execute permissions.
4. If the checks succeed, combine the physical page number and unchanged offset to form the physical address.
pitfalls: A valid page mapping is not enough if the requested access type is forbidden.
A failed check causes an exception, not an arbitrary physical address.
related: Page number, offset, and physical frame
entries.heading: Übersetzungsvorgang – Folie 72

entries.short: Multilevel page tables allocate lower-level tables only for portions of the virtual address space that are actually used.
entries.explanation: A single-level Sv32 table requires `2^20` entries of 4 bytes each, or 4 MiB per process, even when many virtual regions are unused. Multilevel tables split the virtual page number into indices and allocate lower-level tables as needed. Sv32 has two levels with a 10+10+12-bit split; Sv39 has three with a 9+9+9+12-bit split, Sv48 has four, and Sv57 has five. A leaf entry can map a large page directly; in Sv32, that is 4 MiB.
entries.example: If an entry at the first Sv32 level is invalid, no second table needs to be provided for the corresponding address region.
pitfalls: More levels save table space for unused regions but require several memory accesses during a page-table walk.
A leaf entry maps a page directly; a non-leaf entry points to another page-table level.
entries.heading: Warum mehrere Stufen?

entries.short: Sv32 splits a virtual address into two 10-bit page-table indices and a 12-bit offset.
entries.explanation: Sv32 uses two page-table levels: `VPN[1]` selects an entry in the first table, `VPN[0]` selects an entry in the second table, and the lowest 12 bits form the offset. For `VA = 0x00403ABC`, the indices are 1 and 3 and the offset is `0xABC`. If the physical page number is `0x12345`, the physical address is `0x12345 · 0x1000 + 0xABC = 0x12345ABC`.
entries.example: `VPN[1]=1`, `VPN[0]=3`, `Offset=0xABC`; with physical page number `0x12345`, `PA=0x12345ABC`.
pitfalls: Each of the two Sv32 indices is 10 bits wide; the offset is 12 bits.
The virtual page number is translated, while the offset remains unchanged.
related: Page number, offset, and physical frame
entries.heading: Rechenbeispiel Sv32

entries.short: A TLB is a fast cache for recently used virtual-to-physical address translations.
entries.explanation: On a TLB hit, a stored translation can be reused instead of reading all page-table levels again. Without a TLB, an Sv39 translation requires three page-table accesses in addition to the actual data access. On a TLB miss, the translation is looked up in the page tables; an invalid entry or unauthorized access can still cause an exception. Large pages can cover a larger memory region with a single TLB entry.
entries.example: A repeated access to the same virtual page can use the translation already stored in the TLB.
pitfalls: A TLB stores translations; it does not replace the page table as the authoritative mapping.
A TLB hit does not override access permissions.
entries.heading: TLB – Translation Look-Aside Buffer

entries.short: With lazy allocation, a physical frame is assigned only when a virtual page is accessed for the first time.
entries.explanation: The operating system initially reserves virtual address space without immediately assigning a physical frame. The first access to the unmapped page triggers an exception. The handler finds a free frame, sets up the mapping, and then allows execution to resume.
entries.example:
1. Reserve a virtual memory region without physical frames.
2. Handle the exception triggered by the first access.
3. Assign a frame and update the page-table entry.
pitfalls: With lazy allocation, the exception on first access can be expected behavior.
Virtual memory is reserved before the first access, but it is not necessarily backed by physical memory yet.
entries.heading: Lazy Allocation

entries.short: In paging, a selected page is evicted to secondary storage and loaded back in when accessed later.
entries.explanation: If no physical frame is free, the operating system can select a rarely used page, mark it as not present, and write it to secondary storage. The freed frame is assigned to a needed page. If a program later accesses the evicted page, an exception is triggered; the operating system loads the page back and updates the page table. Paging makes main memory appear larger but causes slow accesses.
entries.example:
1. Select a page B that has been unused for a long time and evict it.
2. Assign its frame to a needed page A.
3. When B is accessed later, load the page back and update the mapping.
pitfalls: Eviction to secondary storage is considerably slower than accessing main memory.
Selecting a page for eviction must account for its possible future reuse.
entries.heading: Paging: Auslagern, wenn keine Kachel frei ist

entries.short: Pinned pages remain in physical memory and are not evicted.
entries.explanation: The operating system pins pages when they must remain physically available while in use. Examples include memory regions for devices without an MMU, such as network cards or GPUs, as well as parts of the operating system such as page tables. Pinned pages are not available as eviction candidates during ordinary paging.
entries.example: A page table can be pinned so that the operating system always finds it in main memory during address translation.
pitfalls: Pinned does not automatically mean that a page is accessible to user programs.
Pinning reduces the memory available for ordinary paging.
entries.heading: Paging: Auslagern, wenn keine Kachel frei ist

entries.short: Page-table permissions can be set deliberately so that certain accesses trigger an exception.
entries.explanation: The operating system can revoke read, write, or execute permissions to catch unauthorized accesses. During debugging, this can help detect array overflows or underflows. Protection bits can also be used for performance analysis, for example to count accesses.
entries.example: A read-only page can catch a write attempt and make a program error visible.
pitfalls: A protection fault indicates a forbidden access, but does not automatically identify its cause in the source code.
Access protection relies on the page permissions that have been set.
entries.heading: Zugriffsschutz gezielt nutzen

entries.short: In Little Endian, the least significant byte of a multibyte value is stored at the lowest memory address.
entries.explanation: Byte order determines how the bytes of a multibyte value are arranged in memory. In Little Endian, the byte containing the least significant bits comes first; in Big Endian, the most significant byte comes first. This order concerns how a value is represented in memory, not how a virtual address is split into a page number and offset.
entries.example: The 32-bit value `0x12345678` is stored byte by byte in Little Endian as `78 56 34 12` at increasing addresses.
pitfalls: Little Endian reverses the order of the bytes, not the bit order within each byte.
Endianness and virtual page translation describe different aspects of a memory access.
